sections.heading: 1.1 Minus times minus
sections.excerpt: Losing a debt is a gain. Take away 3 debts of ₹50 and the shop is ₹150 better off. That is what (−3) × (−50) = +150 says: three lots of owing fifty, removed.

steps.text: A shop owes its supplier ₹50 on each of 3 bills. The supplier cancels all 3 bills. Is the shop better or worse off, and by how much?
Losing a debt is a gain. Take away 3 debts of ₹50 and the shop is ₹150 better off. That is what (−3) × (−50) = +150 says: three lots of owing fifty, removed.

Stand at 0 on a number line, facing the positive numbers. Multiplying by −1 means turn around. Turn around once and you face the negative numbers. Turn around twice and you face forward again. In the figure, set the turns to 0, 1 and 2 and watch the arrow.

Why must the answer be positive? Follow this pattern. 3 × (−2) = −6. 2 × (−2) = −4. 1 × (−2) = −2. 0 × (−2) = 0. Each answer is 2 more than the one before. Keep going, and the pattern forces (−1) × (−2) = +2 and (−2) × (−2) = +4. Any other answer would break the pattern.

Numbers with a direction, like +5 and −5, are called directed numbers. The rule has two parts. Same signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer. Dividing follows the same rule, because dividing undoes multiplying.
Work out (−4) × 6 ÷ (−3). First the size: 4 × 6 = 24, and 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Now the signs. There are two minus signs, which is two about-turns. You finish facing forward, so the answer is +8.

The rule is for multiplying and dividing only. −3 − 4 is not +7. It is −7, because you start at −3 and move 4 further left. The saying “two minuses make a plus” tempts you to use the rule where it does not belong. When you add or subtract, walk it on the number line.
Multiplying by a negative number is an about-turn, so two of them leave you facing forward.

sections.heading: 1.2 Every number has an ingredients list
sections.excerpt: 24 splits into equal rows of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 or 12. 23 only works as one long row. Some numbers break into smaller pieces. Others refuse to break at all.

steps.text: A class of 24 can line up in equal rows in many ways. A class of 23 cannot, however you try. What makes 23 so awkward?
24 splits into equal rows of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 or 12. 23 only works as one long row. Some numbers break into smaller pieces. Others refuse to break at all.

Break 60 into two pieces that multiply to make it: 6 × 10. Break those again. 6 is 2 × 3 and 10 is 2 × 5. Now nothing breaks any further. You are left with 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Drawn on paper, this looks like a tree with 60 at the top.

Start a different way: 60 = 4 × 15. Then 4 is 2 × 2 and 15 is 3 × 5. You get 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 again. Whichever way you break a number, you finish with the same unbreakable pieces. They are the number's ingredients list, and every number has exactly one.

A number that divides exactly into another is called a factor. 6 and 10 are factors of 60. A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is a prime number. The unbreakable pieces of 60 are its prime factors, and the drawing is a factor tree. 1 is not prime, because it has only one factor.
Write 84 as a product of prime factors. 84 = 2 × 42. 42 = 2 × 21. 21 = 3 × 7. Every piece is now prime. So 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. Check by multiplying back: 4 × 21 = 84.

It is tempting to stop too early. 84 = 4 × 21 is true, but 4 and 21 can both still break. Keep going until every piece is prime. A second trap is to think every odd number is prime. 9, 15 and 21 are odd, and none of them is prime.
Write 90 as a product of prime factors.
Every whole number bigger than 1 is either prime or built from primes in exactly one way.

sections.heading: 1.3 What two numbers share
sections.excerpt: The number of bunches must divide exactly into 24 and into 36. 2 bunches work. So do 3, 4, 6 and 12. The biggest that works is 12, with 2 roses and 3 marigolds in each bunch.

steps.text: A florist has 24 roses and 36 marigolds. She wants identical bunches with no flowers left over. What is the largest number of bunches she can make?
The number of bunches must divide exactly into 24 and into 36. 2 bunches work. So do 3, 4, 6 and 12. The biggest that works is 12, with 2 roses and 3 marigolds in each bunch.

Use the ingredients lists. 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Both lists contain two 2s and one 3. Those shared pieces multiply to 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. In the figure, set the two numbers to 24 and 36 and read the blue bar.

Why do the shared pieces give the biggest answer? A number divides into 24 only if all its pieces are in 24's list. To divide into both numbers, its pieces must be in both lists. Take every shared piece and you have the biggest such number.

The biggest number that divides into both is the highest common factor, or HCF. Now turn the question round. The numbers in a times table are called multiples. 24, 48 and 72 are multiples of 24. The smallest number in both times tables is the lowest common multiple, or LCM. For 24 and 36 it is 72, the amber bar.

Two buses leave the depot together. One leaves every 12 minutes and the other every 18. When do they next leave together? The multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36. The multiples of 18 are 18, 36. They meet at 36 minutes, so the LCM of 12 and 18 is 36. With prime factors: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. Take each prime the most times it appears in either list. That gives 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36.

The tempting shortcut for the LCM is to multiply the two numbers. 12 × 18 = 216 is a common multiple, but it is not the lowest. Multiplying counts the shared pieces twice. In fact HCF × LCM always equals the two numbers multiplied together. Here 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18.
Find the LCM of 8 and 12.
The HCF is built from the prime pieces two numbers share, and the LCM from every piece either one needs.

sections.heading: 1.4 A shorthand for repeated multiplying
sections.excerpt: Each round doubles the one before: 2, 4, 8, 16. Round 10 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which is 1,024 people. Writing ten 2s is slow and hard to check. We need a shorthand.

steps.text: You forward a message to 2 friends. Each of them forwards it to 2 more, and so on. How many people receive it in the 10th round?
Each round doubles the one before: 2, 4, 8, 16. Round 10 is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which is 1,024 people. Writing ten 2s is slow and hard to check. We need a shorthand.
Write the count of 2s as a small raised number: 2¹⁰. Now look at 2³ × 2². Written out, that is (2 × 2 × 2) × (2 × 2). Count the 2s. There are five, so 2³ × 2² = 2⁵.
Multiplying joins two chains of 2s into one longer chain, so the counts add. Dividing cancels 2s from the chain, so the counts subtract. 2⁵ ÷ 2² removes two of the five 2s and leaves 2³.

2¹⁰ is called a power of 2. The 2 is the base and the small 10 is the index. The plural of index is indices. The counting shortcuts are the laws of indices. To multiply powers of the same base, add the indices. To divide, subtract them.

Simplify 3⁴ × 3² ÷ 3³. Multiplying adds: 4 + 2 = 6, giving 3⁶. Dividing subtracts: 6 − 3 = 3, giving 3³. And 3³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Now try 5² ÷ 5². Subtracting the indices gives 5⁰. But any number divided by itself is 1. So 5⁰ = 1.
There are two traps. First, 2³ is not 2 × 3. It is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Second, the laws need the same base. 2³ × 3² is two different chains, so work out each one: 8 × 9 = 72.
Write 7³ × 7⁵ as a single power of 7.
A power counts how many times a number is multiplied by itself, so multiplying powers adds the counts.

sections.heading: 1.5 The number no fraction can reach
sections.excerpt: For 49, you need a number that multiplies by itself to give 49. That is 7. For 2, try 1.4. 1.4 × 1.4 = 1.96, which is a little too small. Try 1.5. 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25, which is too big. The side is somewhere between.

steps.text: A square garden has an area of 49 square metres. How long is each side? Now make the area 2 square metres. How long is each side this time?

For 49, you need a number that multiplies by itself to give 49. That is 7. For 2, try 1.4. 1.4 × 1.4 = 1.96, which is a little too small. Try 1.5. 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25, which is too big. The side is somewhere between.
Zoom in. 1.41 × 1.41 = 1.9881. 1.42 × 1.42 = 2.0164. So the side is between 1.41 and 1.42. Each extra decimal place gets closer to 2. None of them ever lands on it exactly.

Could some fraction land on it exactly? Suppose one did, written in its lowest terms. Then top × top would equal 2 × bottom × bottom. That makes top × top even, so top is even. Write top as 2 × something, and the same line shows that bottom is even too. But a fraction in its lowest terms cannot have both parts even. So no fraction works. This argument is more than 2,000 years old.

The number that multiplies by itself to give 49 is the square root of 49, written √49 = 7. Numbers that can be written as fractions are called rational. Numbers that cannot, like √2, are called irrational numbers. Their decimals never end and never repeat.
Between which two whole numbers does √50 lie? 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64. 50 is between 49 and 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8. It is only a little above 7, because 50 is only a little above 49.
√16 is 4, not 8. Halving is tempting because it also makes a number smaller. Check by multiplying back: 4 × 4 = 16, but 8 × 8 = 64.
√30 lies between two whole numbers. What is the smaller one?
A square root asks what number times itself gives this one, and most of the answers cannot be written as fractions.

chapters.hookSummary: In a true histogram, the area of each bar — not its height — represents frequency.

intuitionToFormula.concreteAction: Change the width Δx of a histogram class interval and watch the bar height adjust so its area stays equal to frequency f.

intuitionToFormula.formulaDisplay: Frequency Density = f / Δx,   μ = (∑ xᵢ) / n,   σ = √[ (∑(xᵢ − μ)²) / n ]

chapters.title: Updating Belief: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem
chapters.subtitle: Advanced Probability · Atlas Bayes Explorer: why a positive result from a 95% accurate test on a 2% condition is right only 28% of the time
chapters.hookSummary: Evidence never acts in a vacuum — it slices and renormalizes the prior base rate inside a 1,000-person unit square.

intuitionToFormula.concreteAction: Open the Bayes Unit-Square Explorer (`statistics/bayes`): set prevalence p = 2%, sensitivity = 95%, false-positive rate = 5%, and screen 1,000 people.
intuitionToFormula.ahaInvariant: Conditioning on a positive test throws away everyone who tested negative! What remains is just two bars: 19 True Positives (red) from the 20 sick people, and 49 False Positives (amber) from the 980 healthy people — so P(D | +) = 19 / (19 + 49) ≈ 27.9%!

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · Turning round on the number line
atlasLessons.question: What does multiplying by −1 do to a number?
atlasLessons.explanation: It keeps the size and turns the direction round. 3 becomes −3, and −3 becomes 3.
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · What two numbers share
atlasLessons.question: How do the HCF and the LCM of 24 and 36 come from their prime factors?
atlasLessons.explanation: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. The shared primes give the HCF, 12. Every prime either number needs gives the LCM, 72.
atlasLessons.limits: The check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · Why the check always works
atlasLessons.question: Why does HCF × LCM equal the two numbers multiplied together?
atlasLessons.explanation: 24 × 36 uses every prime of both numbers. The LCM takes each prime the most times it appears in either number. The HCF takes the shared ones, which are exactly the primes the LCM left out. Between them they use every prime once.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: HCF × LCM = a × b
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

stories: Evidence never acts in a vacuum — it slices and renormalizes the prior base rate inside a 1,000-person unit square.

atlasLessons.title: Ch 16.2 · Updating Belief: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem (The Visual 'Aha!' Invariant)
atlasLessons.question: What stays constant in Updating Belief: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Theorem when you deform or slice the figure?
atlasLessons.explanation: Conditioning on a positive test throws away everyone who tested negative! What remains is just two bars: 19 True Positives (red) from the 20 sick people, and 49 False Positives (amber) from the 980 healthy people — so P(D | +) = 19 / (19 + 49) ≈ 27.9%!
stories: Evidence never acts in a vacuum — it slices and renormalizes the prior base rate inside a 1,000-person unit square.

atlasLessons.question: How does touching the geometry of Slicing to Infinity: Riemann Sums & The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus reveal its structure?
atlasLessons.explanation: Open the Atlas Calculus (`maths/calculus` pp. 3–5) and compare the blue area under f′(t) = t from 0 to x with the red height of the parabola f(x) = ½x².

stories: Adding up infinitely many thin rate-times-time slivers reconstructs total change: integration and differentiation undo each other.

atlasLessons.question: What stays constant in Slicing to Infinity: Riemann Sums & The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus when you deform or slice the figure?
atlasLessons.explanation: Every tiny step dt adds a ribbon of area f′(t)·dt = df — which is the exact tiny rise in height of the original curve f(x)! That is why the area under the slope curve IS the height change f(b) − f(a)!
atlasLessons.limits: Formula: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim_{n→∞} ∑ f(xᵢ) Δx = F(b) − F(a)   where F′(x) = f(x)

widgets.title: Turning round on the number line
widgets.challengePrompt: Predict where the arrow points after 0, 1 and 2 turns. Then set the turns and check.
widgets.cutaway: Each × (−1) turns the arrow to face the other way. Its length stays the same. Two turns bring it back, so (−1) × (−1) = +1.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the turns to 1. The arrow faces the negative numbers.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Set the turns to 2. The arrow faces forward again, the same length as before.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: The green arrow faces the positive numbers. The red arrow faces the negative numbers.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: On paper, try 3 turns and then 4. Odd counts face backward. Even counts face forward.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch the number line and the two turns in your journal.

widgets.title: What two numbers share
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the two numbers to 24 and 36. Predict the HCF and the LCM, then read the bars.
widgets.cutaway: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. The shared primes give the HCF, 12. Every prime either number needs gives the LCM, 72.
widgets.idealised: The check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the first number to 24 and the second to 36.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The blue bar shows the HCF, 12. The amber bar shows the LCM, 72.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Blue is what the two numbers share. Amber is the smallest number both divide into.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set both numbers to 24. The HCF and the LCM are both 24. Can you say why?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the factor trees for 24 and 36 in your journal and circle the shared primes.

widgets.title: The doubling staircase
widgets.challengePrompt: On paper, write 2¹ to 2¹⁰ as a staircase, each step double the one before. Use it to check that 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ without multiplying it out.
widgets.cutaway: Going up one step multiplies by 2. Going up 3 steps and then 4 more is 7 steps. That is why the indices add.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: 2³ is 8 and 2⁴ is 16. 8 × 16 = 128, which is the 7th step.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 3 steps and then 4 more steps make 7 steps: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Go down instead. 2⁷ ÷ 2⁴ is 4 steps down from the 7th step. Where do you land?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the staircase in your journal and mark the jump from 2³ to 2⁷.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 3 · Surface-Area-to-Volume Ratio (6L² vs L³)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why Elephants Have Huge Ears & Cells Stay Microscopic (SA:V Scaling)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: When a cell or organism enlarges by linear scale factor k, its surface area grows as k² while its metabolising volume grows as k³ — so SA/V = 6/L drops inversely with size.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: SA = 6L²,   V = L³   ⇒   SA : V = 6 / L
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: If a cubical cell doubles its side length from L = 1 μm to L = 2 μm (k = 2), by what factor does its Surface-Area-to-Volume ratio change?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Surface area multiplies by 2² = 4 and volume by 2³ = 8, so SA:V halves from 6:1 to 3:1.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 13 · Mendel's Punnett Squares & Clinical Screening
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Punnett Grids Are 2×2 Area Diagrams & Medical Tests Obey Bayes' Rule
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: A Punnett square for Aa × Aa is literally the algebraic expansion (0.5A + 0.5a)² = 0.25AA + 0.50Aa + 0.25aa, and genetic carrier screening relies on Bayes' theorem.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: In a cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa), given that an offspring shows the dominant phenotype (AA or Aa), what is the conditional probability it is a carrier (Aa)?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Out of 3 dominant-phenotype boxes (1 AA and 2 Aa), 2 are Aa, so P(Aa | Dominant) = 2/3.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: How iPad GPUs Rotate 3D Worlds with Matrices & CPUs Think with De Morgan Gates

crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: R_θ = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]],   ¬(P ∧ Q) ⇔ (¬P) ∨ (¬Q)

schoolQuestions.prompt: Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 72 and 120 using prime factorisation, and verify that HCF × LCM = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1 (Prime Factor Trees): 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3¹ × 5¹.
Step 2 (Venn Intersection = HCF): Take min powers: 2³ × 3¹ = 24.
Step 3 (Venn Union = LCM): Take max powers: 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360.
Step 4 (Invariant Check): 24 × 360 = 8640 = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: HCF = 24 and LCM = 360 because 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; their overlap is 2³ × 3 = 24 and their union is 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

mistakes.name: You mixed up HCF and LCM
mistakes.nextStep: The HCF takes the lower power of each shared prime and the LCM the higher power of every prime, so check which rule you used for each.

mistakes.name: You took the LCM as the numbers multiplied together
mistakes.nextStep: The LCM uses each prime once at its highest power, so rebuild it from the two prime factor lists.

stuck.sister: Find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18 using prime factors.

steps.prompt: Write 12 as a product of prime factors, using powers.
Now write 18 the same way.
The HCF takes each shared prime at its lower power. What is the HCF of 12 and 18?
steps.working: Both numbers share one 2 and one 3, so the HCF is 2 × 3 = 6.

mistakes.name: You mixed up HCF and LCM
mistakes.nextStep: For the HCF take the lower power of each prime both numbers share.

steps.prompt: The LCM takes every prime at its higher power. What is the LCM?
steps.working: The higher powers are 2² and 3², so the LCM is 4 × 9 = 36.

mistakes.name: You took the LCM as the numbers multiplied together
mistakes.nextStep: Multiplying gives a common multiple, but the LCM uses each prime once at its higher power.

mistakes.name: You mixed up HCF and LCM
mistakes.nextStep: For the LCM take the higher power of every prime.

polyaStages.title: 1. Understand the Problem
polyaStages.subtitle: Name what you want, what you're given, and the smaller questions hiding inside
prompts: What am I trying to find? Can I name it, or draw it as a bar?
What facts am I given, and what stays the same? Look for facts hiding in words like 'constant', 'bisects' or 'regular'.
What smaller questions hide inside this one? List the pieces.
polyaStages.exampleProblem: A train passes a 300 m platform in 24 seconds and passes a standing lamp-post in 9 seconds at constant speed. Find the length of the train.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Want: the train's length L. Given: the lamp-post takes 9 s (the train's own length), the platform takes 24 s (the train plus 300 m), and the speed never changes. Pieces: the train's speed, and how long the 300 m takes on its own.

polyaStages.title: 2. Devise a Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Pick the piece you can crack right now. If none gives, change the picture: a bar model, a smaller version, working backwards, or symmetry
prompts: Which piece can I solve right now, with only what I'm given? Start there.
If no piece gives way, can I draw a bar model, or add a helper line to the figure?
Can I try a smaller version first (n = 1, 2, 3), or work backwards from what I want?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Put the train's two journeys on one bar and look for a piece you can solve.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Piece found: the extra 300 m. Bar 1 is [train] and takes 9 s. Bar 2 is [train] + [300 m] and takes 24 s. So the 300 m on its own takes 24 − 9 = 15 s. We can crack that now: it's the foothold.

polyaStages.title: 3. Carry Out the Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Crack the foothold, then use its answer to open the next piece, until the whole problem gives
prompts: What did my first piece give me, and which piece does it open next?
Does each step follow from the line above it?
Are my units and signs still right? Can I say what each middle number means?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Use the 15-second piece to find the speed, then the speed to find L.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Piece solved: 300 m in 15 s, so the speed is 300 ÷ 15 = 20 m/s. Piece used: the lamp-post takes 9 s at 20 m/s. Whole solved: L = 20 × 9 = 180 m.

polyaStages.title: 4. Look Back & Generalise
polyaStages.subtitle: Check the answer, check the pieces fit back together, and keep the move for next time
prompts: Does the answer work in the original problem?
Did my pieces fit back together? Which piece was the key one, and how did I spot it?
Can I write a rule for any platform length P and times t₁ and t₂?
Where else could 'compare two cases and subtract' find me a foothold?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Check L = 180 m, name the key piece, and write the rule.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Check: (180 + 300) ÷ 20 = 24 s ✓. Key piece: the extra 300 m, found by comparing the two journeys. Rule: L = P · t₁ ÷ (t₂ − t₁).

visualMathTips.title: Why minus times minus is plus
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Multiplying by −1 turns you round on the number line.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Two about-turns leave you facing the way you started.

visualMathTips.title: Why (a + b)² ≠ a² + b²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Draw a square of side (a + b) and slice it into 4 rectangles.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Besides the corner squares a² and b², two blue rectangles of area ab sit on the sides — forgetting 2ab leaves two big holes in the square!

visualMathTips.title: Why 1 + 2 + … + n = ½n(n + 1)
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Build a staircase of 1, 2, …, n blocks, clone it, and flip the clone upside-down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The two staircases interlock into a solid rectangle of width n and height (n + 1)!

visualMathTips.title: Why a Circle's Area Is πr²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Slice a circle into 24 pizza sectors and comb them together alternating up and down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The wavy top and bottom each use half the circumference (πr), while the height is the radius r — forming a rectangle of base πr and height r!

visualMathTips.title: Why sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for Every Angle
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: On the unit circle of radius 1, level light casts vertical shadow sin θ and top light casts horizontal shadow cos θ.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Those two shadows are the legs of a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 — so their squares always add to 1² = 1!

visualMathTips.title: Why a Positive Result from a 95% Accurate Test Is Wrong 72% of the Time
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: In the 1,000-person unit square at 2% prevalence, only 20 people are sick while 980 are healthy.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: 5% false alarms on 980 healthy people creates 49 false positives (amber), dwarfing the 19 true positives (red)!

visualMathTips.title: Why Slope and Area Are Inverses (FTC)
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Compare the blue triangle of area under f′(t) = t with the red height bar of f(x) = ½x².
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Each thin strip of area f′(t)·dt equals df — the tiny vertical step of the original curve. Summing all tiny rises gives total height f(x) − f(0)!

visualMathTips.title: Why det(A) = ad − bc Is Area
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Drag the red basis vector Aî = (a, c) and blue basis vector Aĵ = (b, d) in the 2×2 Matrix Sandbox.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The unit 1×1 square deforms into a parallelogram whose bounding box (a+b)(c+d), minus four right triangles and two b×c rectangles, leaves exact area ad − bc!

footings.skill: Multiply and divide negative numbers
footings.teach: Same signs make a positive and different signs make a negative, so (−3) × (−2) = 6 and 6 ÷ (−3) = −2, and a minus sign stays with its number through every step. Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number turns the sign round: −x < 2 becomes x > −2.

probes.prompt: Work out 2 × 3 − 4 × 5.
Solve −2x < 8.

footings.skill: Undo each step with its inverse
footings.teach: Undo the last step first and do the same to both sides: for x/2 + 3 = 8, take 3 from both sides to get x/2 = 5, then multiply by 2 to get x = 10. An inverse function f⁻¹ makes those undo steps; it is not 1 ÷ f.

probes.prompt: Solve x + 9 = 4.
Solve x/4 − 3 = 2.
f(x) = 2x + 1. Find f⁻¹(9).

footings.skill: Multiply every term inside a bracket
footings.teach: The number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside it: −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12. A squared bracket is two brackets, so (x + 2)² = (x + 2)(x + 2) = x² + 4x + 4, not x² + 4.

probes.prompt: Expand −2(x − 5).
Expand (x + 3)².
Work out 7² − 3², then (7 − 3)².

footings.skill: Find the HCF and LCM, and cancel fully
footings.teach: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both, and the LCM is the smallest number both divide into: for 4 and 10, the HCF is 2 and the LCM is 20, not 4 × 10 = 40. Cancel a fraction by the HCF so nothing common is left, as in 10/15 = 2/3.

probes.prompt: Find the LCM of 6 and 8.
Find the HCF of 18 and 24.
Write 18/24 in its simplest form.

footings.skill: Square a number and undo it with a square root
footings.teach: Squaring multiplies a number by itself, so 5² = 5 × 5 = 25, not 10, and a square root undoes it: √25 = 5. In a right-angled triangle, square the two shorter sides, add, then take the square root: 3² + 4² = 25, so the longest side is 5.

probes.prompt: Work out 6².
x² = 64 and x is positive. Find x.
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the longest side.

footings.skill: Use a common denominator and improper fractions
footings.teach: Add or subtract fractions only once they share a denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, never 2/5. Turn a mixed number into an improper fraction first, so 1 1/2 is 3/2.

probes.prompt: Work out 1/3 + 1/4.
Work out 2 1/3 − 1 2/3.
Work out 2 1/2 × 1 1/5.

footings.skill: Round to decimal places and significant figures
footings.teach: Look at the digit after the last one you keep and round up if it is 5 or more, so 2.367 to 2 decimal places is 2.37, not 2.36. Significant figures start at the first digit that is not zero: 0.005281 to 2 significant figures is 0.0053.

probes.prompt: Round 4.2861 to 2 decimal places.
Round 0.07368 to 2 significant figures.
Round 52,718 to 2 significant figures.

footings.skill: Multiply and divide by 10, 100 and decimals
footings.teach: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left, so 0.47 × 100 = 47, and a recurring decimal never stops, so 10 × 0.333… take away 0.333… is exactly 3. To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 until it is whole: 12 ÷ 0.3 = 120 ÷ 3 = 40.

probes.prompt: Work out 0.36 × 100.
Work out 36 ÷ 0.4.
x = 0.555…, where the fives go on for ever. Work out 10x − x.

footings.skill: Choose multiply or divide, and which way round
footings.teach: Ask what one of something is worth: if 4 pens cost £6, one pen costs 6 ÷ 4 = £1.50, and the amount you share out goes first. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger answer, so 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4.

probes.prompt: A car goes 75 km on 6 litres of fuel. How far does it go on 1 litre?
How many 0.25 kg bags can be filled from 3 kg of rice?
A 1.5 m ribbon is cut into pieces 0.3 m long. How many pieces are there?

footings.skill: Work out what one part is worth
footings.teach: Find one part first: to share 45 in the ratio 4 : 5, there are 9 parts, so one part is 5 and the shares are 20 and 25. If more workers do the same job, it takes less time: 2 workers taking 6 hours means 1 worker takes 12 hours.

probes.prompt: Share 60 in the ratio 2 : 3.
4 workers paint a fence in 6 days. How long would 8 workers take at the same rate?
Two amounts are in the ratio 2 : 5. The larger is 15 more than the smaller. What is the smaller amount?

footings.skill: Use a multiplier for a percentage change
footings.teach: A percentage change is one multiplication: a 30% decrease is × 0.7 and a 5% increase is × 1.05. Two changes multiply, so up 40% then down 40% is × 1.4 × 0.6 = × 0.84, and to undo a change you divide by its multiplier.

probes.prompt: What do you multiply by to decrease an amount by 15%?
A price rises by 10%, then rises by 10% again. What single multiplier does the same?
After a 20% increase, a coat costs £60. What did it cost before the increase?

footings.skill: Convert units, and square the factor for areas
footings.teach: Change every length to the same unit before you calculate: 1 m = 100 cm, so 3.2 m = 320 cm. An area scales by the square of the length factor, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm², and doubling every length makes an area 4 times as big.

probes.prompt: Write 2.5 m in centimetres.
How many cm² are there in 3 m²?
A shape has area 5 cm². It is enlarged by scale factor 3. What is its new area?

footings.skill: Use the right lengths in area and perimeter
footings.teach: A triangle's area is half of base × perpendicular height, so base 6 cm and height 4 cm give 12 cm², and a slanted side is never the height. Use the radius in πr², and add every edge for a perimeter: a quarter circle of radius 2 cm has perimeter π + 4.

probes.prompt: A triangle has base 12 cm, a slanted side 10 cm and perpendicular height 8 cm. Find its area.
A semicircle has diameter 10 cm. Find its perimeter, using π = 3.14.
A circle has diameter 12 cm. Find its area in terms of π.

footings.skill: Use angle facts for parallel lines, polygons and bearings
footings.teach: Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°, and an exterior angle of a polygon is 180° take away the interior angle, so an interior angle of 108° has exterior angle 72°. A back-bearing is the bearing plus 180°, or minus 180° if that passes 360°: the back-bearing of 050° is 230°.

probes.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 115°. Find the other.
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. What is each exterior angle?
The bearing of B from A is 120°. What is the bearing of A from B?

footings.skill: Find a midpoint and a gradient from coordinates
footings.teach: The midpoint averages the x-coordinates and then the y-coordinates, keeping x first: the midpoint of (1, 2) and (5, 10) is (3, 6). Gradient is change in y ÷ change in x, and a perpendicular gradient flips it and changes its sign, so 2/3 becomes −3/2.

probes.prompt: Find the midpoint of (2, 3) and (8, 11).
Find the gradient of the line through (2, 1) and (5, 13).
A line has gradient 3. What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to it?

footings.skill: Reflect, rotate and enlarge a point
footings.teach: Check the mirror line or centre before you move: reflecting (3, 4) in the y-axis gives (−3, 4), and a 90° turn clockwise about the origin takes (x, y) to (y, −x). To enlarge about a centre, multiply the step from the centre to the point, then add it back on: (3, 2) from centre (1, 1) by scale factor 3 is (7, 4).

probes.prompt: Reflect the point (2, 5) in the x-axis.
Rotate the point (3, 1) through 90° clockwise about the origin.
Enlarge the point (4, 3) by scale factor 2, centre (1, 1).

footings.skill: List equally likely outcomes and count each once
footings.teach: List every outcome so each one is equally likely: a coin and a spinner numbered 1 to 3 give H1, H2, H3, T1, T2 and T3, six outcomes. When order does not matter, a pair like AB is the same as BA, so count it once.

probes.prompt: Two fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of one head and one tail?
Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 3?
How many different pairs can you choose from 4 people, if order does not matter?

footings.skill: Use the right total for a probability
footings.teach: The total is the group you are picking from at that moment. If 1 of 10 sweets is eaten, the next pick is out of 9, and if you are told the person wears glasses, the total is only the people who wear glasses.

probes.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue counters. A red counter is taken out and not put back. What is the probability that the next counter is red?
In a club of 20, 12 play football and 3 of those also play chess. A football player is picked at random. What is the probability that they play chess?
In a class of 30, 15 wear glasses and 10 are left-handed. 5 are left-handed and wear glasses. A student who wears glasses is picked. What is the probability they are left-handed?

footings.skill: Find class width, frequency density and quartiles
footings.teach: Class width is the upper boundary take away the lower one, and frequency density is frequency ÷ class width: 10 ≤ x < 40 has width 30, so frequency 60 gives density 2. The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, not the largest value minus the smallest.

probes.prompt: The class 20 ≤ t < 35 has frequency 45. Find its frequency density.
A histogram bar for 0 ≤ x < 5 has frequency density 4. How many values are in that class?
Find the interquartile range of 1, 3, 8, 9, 12, 20, 24.

footings.skill: Add and subtract column vectors
footings.teach: Add or subtract the top numbers, then the bottom numbers: (2, 5) − (3, 1) = (−1, 4). To go from P to Q, go back to O and then out again, so PQ = −p + q.

probes.prompt: Work out the column vector (3, 2) + (1, −4).
Work out the column vector (5, 1) − (2, 3).
OA = a and OB = b. Write the vector AB in terms of a and b.

footings.skill: Find and use the nth term of a sequence
footings.teach: Sequences start at n = 1, so test a rule by putting n = 1 and n = 2 back in: for 2, 7, 12, … the rule 5n − 3 gives 2, then 7. Counting from 3 to 6 including both ends gives 4 numbers, not 3.

probes.prompt: Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, …
The nth term of a sequence is 4n − 1. Find the 10th term.
How many whole numbers are there from 5 to 12, counting both 5 and 12?

footings.skill: Check you answered what was asked
footings.teach: Before you write the answer, reread the last line of the question. If a = 5 and it asks for 3a − 2, then 5 is only a step and 13 is the answer.

probes.prompt: A shirt costs £20. It is reduced by 15%. What is the new price?
3x = 12. Find the value of 2x + 1.
A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm and length 9 cm. Find its area.

concepts.name: Negative number
concepts.oneSentence: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign in front.
concepts.picture: The night temperature in Shimla is 2 °C. It drops by 5 degrees. It passes zero and lands on −3 °C. On a number line, negative numbers sit to the left of 0.
steps: To add a negative number, move left. 4 + (−6) = −2.
To subtract a negative number, move right. 4 − (−6) = 10.
To multiply or divide, work out the size first. Then count the minus signs.
An even count of minus signs gives a positive answer. An odd count gives a negative answer.
concepts.workedExample: Work out (−6) × 5. The size is 6 × 5 = 30. There is one minus sign, so the answer is negative. (−6) × 5 = −30.

mixUp.name: the take-away sign
mixUp.how: In 7 − 3 the sign is an instruction to take away. In −3 it is part of the number.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Factor
concepts.oneSentence: A number that divides exactly into another number, with nothing left over.
concepts.picture: 24 students can line up in 4 equal rows of 6. So 4 and 6 are both factors of 24. They cannot make 5 equal rows, so 5 is not a factor of 24.
steps: Try dividing by 1, 2, 3 and so on.
Each time it divides exactly, write down the pair. For 24: 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6.
Stop when the pairs start to repeat. The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24.
concepts.workedExample: Find the factors of 18. The pairs are 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6. 4 and 5 do not divide exactly. The next pair would be 6 × 3, which repeats. So the factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.

mixUp.how: The factors of 12 are 12 or smaller. The multiples of 12 are 12 or bigger.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers
Prime number
Prime factors
Highest common factor

concepts.name: Multiple
concepts.oneSentence: What you get when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3 and so on.
concepts.picture: A bus leaves every 6 minutes. It leaves at 6, 12, 18 and 24 minutes past the hour. Those times are the multiples of 6.
steps: Write the number.
Keep adding the same number: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30.
That list is its times table, and it never ends.
concepts.workedExample: Is 42 a multiple of 6? 6 × 7 = 42, so yes. Is 44? 44 ÷ 6 leaves 2 over, so no.

mixUp.how: Multiples of 6 are 6 or bigger: 6, 12, 18. Factors of 6 are 6 or smaller: 1, 2, 3, 6.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers
Lowest common multiple

concepts.name: Prime number
concepts.oneSentence: A whole number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
concepts.picture: 7 students can only line up as 1 row of 7 or 7 rows of 1. No other equal rows work, so 7 is prime. 6 students can make 2 rows of 3, so 6 is not.
steps: Try dividing by 2, 3, 5, 7 and so on.
If nothing divides exactly before the pairs repeat, the number is prime.
Remember that 1 is not prime. It has only one factor.
The first few primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19.
concepts.workedExample: Is 29 prime? It is odd, so 2 does not divide it. 29 ÷ 3 leaves 2 over. 29 ÷ 5 leaves 4 over. 6 × 6 is already more than 29, so there is nothing bigger to check. 29 is prime.

check.prompt: Which of these is prime: 21, 23 or 27?

mixUp.name: odd numbers
mixUp.how: 9, 15 and 21 are odd but not prime. And 2 is prime but not odd.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers
Prime factors

concepts.name: Prime factors
concepts.oneSentence: The prime numbers that multiply together to make a number.
concepts.picture: Think of primes as bricks that cannot be split. 12 is built from the bricks 2, 2 and 3, because 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. No other set of prime bricks makes 12.
steps: Split the number into any two factors. 60 = 6 × 10.
Split each part again until every part is prime. 6 = 2 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5.
Write the primes in order. 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
Check by multiplying back. 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60.
concepts.workedExample: Write 84 as a product of primes. 84 = 2 × 42. 42 = 2 × 21. 21 = 3 × 7. So 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. Starting with 84 = 7 × 12 gives the same four primes.

check.prompt: Write 30 as a product of prime factors.

mixUp.how: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Its prime factors are only 2, 2 and 3.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers
Highest common factor
Lowest common multiple

concepts.name: Highest common factor
concepts.oneSentence: The biggest number that divides exactly into both numbers.
concepts.picture: You have 12 samosas and 18 jalebis. You want identical plates with nothing left over. The most plates you can make is 6, each with 2 samosas and 3 jalebis. So the HCF of 12 and 18 is 6.
steps: List the factors of each number. 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
Find the ones in both lists: 1, 2, 3 and 6.
Take the biggest: 6.
concepts.bigNumbers: Break each number into prime factors. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. They share one 2 and one 3. Multiply what they share: 2 × 3 = 6.
concepts.workedExample: Find the HCF of 16 and 40. 16 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 and 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5. They share three 2s. 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, so the HCF is 8.

check.prompt: What is the HCF of 20 and 30?

mixUp.how: The HCF is never bigger than the smaller number. The LCM is never smaller than the bigger number.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Lowest common multiple
concepts.oneSentence: The smallest number that both numbers divide into exactly.
concepts.picture: One bus leaves every 4 minutes and another every 6 minutes. They leave together now. They next leave together 12 minutes later. So the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
steps: List the multiples of each number. 4: 4, 8, 12, 16. 6: 6, 12, 18.
Find the first number in both lists: 12.
concepts.bigNumbers: Break each number into prime factors. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. Take each prime the most times it appears in either number. That is two 2s and two 3s. 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36.
concepts.workedExample: Find the LCM of 6 and 15. The multiples of 15 are 15, 30, 45. Does 6 divide into 15? No. Into 30? Yes, 6 × 5 = 30. The LCM is 30. Notice that it is not 6 × 15 = 90.

check.prompt: What is the LCM of 6 and 8?

mixUp.how: The LCM is the bigger answer. Both numbers divide into it. The HCF is the smaller answer. It divides into both numbers.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Power
concepts.oneSentence: A short way to write a number multiplied by itself several times.
concepts.picture: You forward a message to 3 people. Each of them forwards it to 3 more. In the 4th round it reaches 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 people. We write that as 3⁴.
steps: The big number is the base. It is the number being multiplied.
The small raised number is the index. It says how many times the base appears.
Write it out and multiply. 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.
concepts.workedExample: Work out 5³. The base is 5 and it appears 3 times. 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers
Laws of indices
Square root

concepts.name: Laws of indices
concepts.oneSentence: Shortcuts for multiplying and dividing powers of the same number.
concepts.picture: 2³ × 2² is (2 × 2 × 2) × (2 × 2). Count the 2s. There are five, so 2³ × 2² = 2⁵.
steps: Check that the bases match. The laws only work for the same base.
To multiply, add the indices. 2³ × 2² = 2⁵.
To divide, subtract the indices. 2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³.
For a power of a power, multiply the indices. (2³)² = 2⁶.
concepts.workedExample: Simplify 3⁴ × 3² ÷ 3³. Multiplying adds the indices, giving 3⁶. Dividing subtracts them, giving 3³. And 3³ = 27.

check.prompt: 5² × 5⁴ is a single power of 5. What is its index?

mixUp.name: different bases
mixUp.how: 2³ × 3² has two different bases, so no law joins it. Work out each part: 8 × 9 = 72.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Square root
concepts.oneSentence: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the number you started with.
concepts.picture: A square floor has 49 tiles. Each side must be 7 tiles long, because 7 × 7 = 49. So the square root of 49 is 7, written √49 = 7.
steps: Ask what number times itself gives this one.
Use the square numbers you know: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
If the number sits between two of them, so does its root. √30 is between 5 and 6.

mixUp.name: halving

Irrational number

concepts.name: Irrational number
concepts.oneSentence: A number that cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.
concepts.picture: Type √2 into a calculator. It shows 1.41421356 and then runs out of screen. The digits never end and never settle into a repeating pattern. No fraction lands exactly on it.
steps: If a number can be written as a fraction, like 0.75 = 3/4, it is rational.
A decimal that stops, or repeats for ever, can always be written as a fraction.
The square root of a whole number that is not a square number is irrational. √2, √3 and √5 are.
concepts.workedExample: Is √36 irrational? No. √36 = 6, a whole number. Is √40 irrational? 40 is not a square number, so yes.

check.prompt: Only one of √16, √20 and √25 is irrational. Which number is under its root sign?

mixUp.name: a long decimal
mixUp.how: 0.333… goes on for ever, but it repeats and equals 1/3. It is rational. An irrational number never repeats.
